beats.caption: Small cells on the lamp posts, many per block
beats.text: Millimetre-wave networks put small radios on street furniture: lamp posts, poles and building faces. Each is a box about the size of a shoebox, and a dense city needs many of them close together.

beats.caption: Inside the module: a patch array printed on a laminate
beats.text: The radio is an antenna-in-package: a grid of tiny patch antennas printed on a laminate, sitting right on top of the beamformer chip. Short traces keep the loss low at these frequencies.

beats.caption: 24 to 100 GHz: a wide channel, but a short reach
beats.text: At these frequencies the wavelength is a few millimetres. Channels are wide, so peak throughput is high, but the waves die out over short distances. A single cell covers a short stretch of street.

beats.caption: A wall or a building blocks the path; a nearer cell takes over
beats.text: Walls, glass, foliage and even people block or absorb these waves. When the path is cut, the network hands the phone to a cell with a clear line, which is why the sites sit so close together.

beats.caption: Dense sites on every block: many small cells, not a few towers
beats.text: The model is many small sites, not a few tall towers. Each cell carries a few hundred metres of street (est.), so carriers need far more sites per square kilometre. Qualcomm (QCOM), Skyworks (SWKS), Qorvo (QRVO) and Verizon (VZ) are named in this build-out.
